landscape_summary:
The AI-engineering education market splits into five camps, and none of them is interview prep. (1) Broad from-scratch courses (rohitg00/ai-engineering-from-scratch: 542 lessons, 20 phases; mlabonne/llm-course; the HF LLM and Agents courses) are free and deep but sprawl into math, CV and speech, with no timed practice, no seniority tags and thin interactivity. (2) Static question banks (amitshekhariitbhu's ~570 questions, guocong-bincai's 28 modules, llmgenai's 119) have good taxonomies, but answers are external links or missing, with no difficulty tags, quizzes, code execution or tracking. (3) Reference books and guides (Chip Huyen's AI Engineering, ombharatiya/ai-system-design-guide with its 147-question bank and 15 case studies) are the closest to interview intent and the canonical syllabus, but they are static and passive. (4) Paid cohorts (Maven evals at $4,200, aiengg.dev, Udemy bootcamps) are valued for accountability and community and are not reusable, not open and not calibrated to interviews. (5) Best-in-class explainers (Transformer Explainer, Alammar, Tiktokenizer, Brilliant, Josh Comeau) prove that interactive teaching works, but they are single-topic, with no graded questions and no path.
What is fragmented: interview formats are new and unlike LeetCode (take-home with an eval report, debug-a-looping-agent, AI-collaborative coding scored on prompt clarity and verification, customer-discovery simulation, LLM system design, hand-written attention), yet nobody drills them. Evals is the highest-value, most-asked skill and sits behind a $4,200 paywall. Inference and serving internals (KV cache, continuous batching) are asked by labs and have no interactive teaching. Security has no interview-oriented content. Company-tagged data is the paywall at LeetCode, NeetCode and Hello Interview.
What nobody does well: a finite ordered path with predict-then-reveal lessons, runnable in-browser graded exercises (Pyodide plus a mock LLM, no API key), three-depth answers with self-rating, spaced repetition, a daily item and streak, rubric-scored system design with live token/cost/latency calculators, company and role tags, and a community loop-report flow, all free, vendor-neutral and static-hosted. Inferview's wedge is to be the practice layer that sits on top of the existing reading material: link out for depth, own the drills, the widgets and the habit loop.
differentiators: Graded, in-browser practice instead of link lists: Pyodide (numpy/pandas/scikit-learn available, no torch) plus a deterministic mock LLM runs hidden tests locally, so no API keys or backend. Evidence: every question bank found (amitshekhariitbhu, llmgenai, guocong-bincai) has no inline answers or execution (https://github.com/amitshekhariitbhu/ai-engineering-interview-questions); Pyodide package list at https://pyodide.org/en/stable/usage/packages-in-pyodide.html

Interview formats as first-class problem types (take-home with recall@5 and faithfulness report, debug-a-looping-agent, AI-collaborative coding scored on prompt clarity/verification/decomposition/judgment, customer-discovery sim, hand-written attention). Evidence: https://www.techinterview.org/post/3233476824/ai-engineer-interview-rag-agents-evals/ and https://www.techinterview.org/post/3233474914/anthropic-interview-process-ai-collaborative-2026/

Free flagship Evals track mapped from the practitioner FAQ structure (error analysis, binary labels, judge validation, CI vs monitoring), against a $4,200 paid cohort. Evidence: https://maven.com/parlance-labs/evals and https://hamel.dev/blog/posts/evals-faq/ (link out and write original content, do not copy)

Real-model widgets, not mock-ups: the model and the visualization are the same object (GPT-2 small via ONNX Runtime Web in Transformer Explainer), plus precomputed fallbacks when WebGPU is missing. Evidence: https://poloclub.github.io/transformer-explainer/ and https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers.js/index

Inference/serving simulators (continuous batching, PagedAttention, KV-cache sizer) as a flagship interactive topic; only static papers and blogs exist. Evidence: https://www.cs.princeton.edu/~ravian/COS597_F24/papers/vllm.pdf and https://github.com/stas00/ml-engineering

Security as a playable track (Gandalf-style levels against a scripted mock model, harden-this-system-prompt exercises, garak-style probe families) where no interview-oriented content exists. Evidence: https://github.com/NVIDIA/garak

Every item tagged by difficulty, seniority, role track and company with provenance and recency, and free; LeetCode, NeetCode and Hello Interview paywall company data and depth. Evidence: https://neetcode.io/roadmap and https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/in-a-hurry/introduction

Three-depth answer mechanic (30-second conclusion, 3-minute with trade-offs, follow-up on verification/failure/alternatives) with self-rating feeding spaced repetition; static in the only repo that has it. Evidence: https://github.com/guocong-bincai/ai-interview-guide

Habit loop missing from every AI-eng resource: deterministic daily problem with archive, forgiving streak, client-side FSRS review ('N cards due'), friend/private leaderboards. Evidence: Anki FAQ on FSRS https://faqs.ankiweb.net/what-spaced-repetition-algorithm and Advent of Code https://adventofcode.com/2024/about

Interview-shaped system-design drills with rubric self-scoring and live token-cost/latency/KV-memory calculators instead of static Mermaid case studies. Evidence: https://github.com/ombharatiya/ai-system-design-guide (15 case studies, static) and rubric themes in https://www.hellointerview.com/learn/system-design/in-a-hurry/introduction

Built for experienced SWEs: skips math/CV/speech, uses software analogies (tokenizer = compiler front end, KV cache = memoization, continuous batching = event loop scheduling), and a 'short on time' crunch path. Evidence: scope bloat in https://github.com/rohitg00/ai-engineering-from-scratch and weighting from JD analysis https://aishippingblog.com/p/what-1000-job-descriptions-reveal

Open-contribution content pipeline: one file per item with Zod-validated frontmatter, stable node IDs, CI link-check and reference-solution tests, split code/content licenses, anonymous loop-report submissions. Evidence: https://github.com/kamranahmedse/developer-roadmap, https://github.com/neetcode-gh/leetcode, https://github.com/anthropics/anthropic-cookbook

curriculum.why: Experienced SWEs know systems, not ML. This track gives just enough internals (tokens, embeddings, attention, sampling, training stages) to reason about cost, latency and failure modes, and to survive the 'explain attention' and 'implement a sampler' rounds. No heavy math; every concept gets a toy-number pass then a real-scale pass.

writing_style_guide: Use a fixed lesson skeleton: hook (a real interview prompt or production incident), intuition with toy numbers, one widget isolating one variable, real-scale numbers, editable code, then an interview question with three-depth answer. Derived from Alammar, Comeau and Distill patterns (https://jalammar.github.io/illustrated-transformer/, https://www.joshwcomeau.com/css/interactive-guide-to-flexbox/).

Predict before you reveal: ask readers to guess the output, token count or failure stage before every widget; it mirrors the interview moment and is evidence-based (Brilliant pretesting https://brilliant.org/about/).
Toy numbers first, real numbers second (4-d vectors, then 4096-d). Always label tensor shapes and units. Show vectors as heatmaps, not digits.

Write for people who ship software: explain with analogies from systems they know (KV cache = memoization, continuous batching = event-loop scheduling, tokenizer = lexer, eval suite = test suite) and never explain what a REST API or a hash map is.

First-person, candid, a little self-deprecating voice with one running metaphor per lesson and a payoff line. Use labelled callouts: 'Interview tip', 'Common trap', 'Production reality', 'Skip this if short on time'.
Anchor each topic in one concrete case study with real failure symptoms and rules of thumb (the Hamel evals pattern https://hamel.dev/blog/posts/evals/) instead of abstract lists.

Every answer has three depths: 30-second conclusion, 3-minute answer with trade-offs, and the follow-ups interviewers ask (how do you verify, how does it fail, what is the alternative). Depth idea from https://github.com/guocong-bincai/ai-interview-guide.
Numbers or it did not happen: every performance, cost or accuracy claim carries a number, an assumption, and a source or 'illustrative' tag. Include latency/price tables with a last-verified date.

Tag every item with difficulty, seniority (new-grad/mid/senior/staff), role track and company, and show provenance (candidate report vs author-written) and recency. Most sources are anecdotal blogs, so label confidence.
Teach trade-offs, not recipes: each concept ends with 'when this is wrong' and 'what I would say in the room'. Prefer vendor-neutral names; name vendors only as examples.

Keep lessons 15-30 minutes with a visible time estimate (DeepLearning.AI-style bite size https://www.deeplearning.ai/short-courses/). Fun comes from interactivity and voice, not memes; keep gamification light so content stays the star.

Original content only: link out to Alammar, Weng, Karpathy, Huyen, Hamel and others for depth instead of copying; record every borrowed idea's license in a SOURCES file (CC-BY-SA material such as https://github.com/stas00/ml-engineering carries share-alike terms).
Every widget has a no-JS / no-WebGPU fallback (recorded output or static figure) and keyboard and screen-reader access; heavy models load only on an explicit button.
Say what is uncertain: mark fast-moving claims with a freshness badge and a 'last verified' date, and avoid unsupported stats.

tech_stack_recommendation.choice: Astro 5 + MDX content collections (Zod-validated frontmatter) + React islands (hydrated with client:visible) + Tailwind, deployed as a static site on Cloudflare Pages; Pyodide in a Web Worker for code exercises, CodeMirror 6 for the editor, js-tiktoken and transformers.js (WASM, q8) lazy-loaded, WebLLM strictly opt-in, Pagefind for search, nanostores plus localStorage/IndexedDB for progress, SRS and streaks (with JSON export/import), pnpm + Turborepo monorepo.
reasons: Zero JS by default means fast reading pages; client:visible lazy-hydrates heavy widgets (Pyodide, tokenizer, WebLLM) only when scrolled into view (https://starlight.astro.build/getting-started/).

Content-as-files with a strict Zod schema (id, title, track, level, prerequisites, estMinutes, tags, companies, type, lastVerified, license) makes contribution a one-file PR and fails the build on bad metadata; mirrors roadmap.sh node-ID files and freeCodeCamp curriculum-as-files (https://github.com/kamranahmedse/developer-roadmap, https://github.com/freeCodeCamp/freeCodeCamp).

Fully static and backend-free: Pyodide runs numpy/pandas/scikit-learn Python exercises (no torch) with hidden tests (https://pyodide.org/en/stable/usage/packages-in-pyodide.html); transformers.js runs small models on WASM with optional WebGPU (https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers.js/index); WebLLM for opt-in chat (https://webllm.mlc.ai/docs/).
Pagefind adds search with under 300kB payload for 10k pages and supports filters by track/difficulty (https://pagefind.app/).

Cloudflare Pages free tier: 500 builds/month, 20k files, 25 MiB per asset, custom _headers, preview deploys per PR (https://developers.cloudflare.com/pages/platform/limits/); GitHub Pages remains a fallback but discourages commercial use and has a 100GB/month soft cap.

Contributor tooling copied from proven repos: registry/authors files, lychee link-check, pre-commit, CONTRIBUTING with a 10-minute 'add a question' path (https://github.com/anthropics/anthropic-cookbook), CI-generated catalog JSON with verification (https://github.com/neetcode-gh/leetcode), and CI that runs every reference solution in Pyodide under Node.

Licensing split from day one: code MIT or Apache-2.0, content CC BY-SA 4.0 (or CC BY), stated plainly in the repo; avoids freeCodeCamp's restrictive curriculum copyright and AGPL platforms such as Exercism's (https://github.com/exercism/website).
alternatives: Fumadocs on Next.js static export (MDX with React components, built-in search): good if the team wants all-React and app-like pages; heavier JS and Next coupling (https://fumadocs.dev/docs).
Astro Starlight as the docs chrome for reference pages, with custom layouts for the problem catalog (https://starlight.astro.build/getting-started/).
SvelteKit or Next.js app for a more app-like practice experience, with a bigger JS payload and weaker static-content ergonomics.

Optional later: GitHub OAuth plus Supabase (RLS) to sync progress across devices; Giscus for per-problem discussion; Sandpack for JS/TS app exercises (https://sandpack.codesandbox.io/docs). Skip WebContainers (proprietary commercial license, COOP/COEP headers, weak non-Chromium support, https://webcontainers.io/guides/browser-support).
risks: Pyodide cold start (10MB+, figure from knowledge) and no PyTorch: preload on idle, design exercises numpy-only, run in a Worker with kill-on-timeout.
WebGPU fragmentation and large first-load model downloads: always opt-in, capability-detect, cache, and ship precomputed fallbacks; never host weights ourselves (use the Hugging Face CDN).
Progress lives in one browser: users lose streaks when switching devices; ship export/import and plan optional sync early.
Content staleness in a fast-moving field and anecdotal interview data: lastVerified dates, CI flagging pages older than N months, provenance labels, and a loop-report flow.
Cloudflare 20,000-file cap versus thousands of problem pages: ship the catalog as chunked JSON and render client-side lists, while keeping canonical pages for SEO.
Cross-island shared state in Astro: use nanostores.

Authoring cost of interactive widgets: build a small reusable library (slider, step-through, token strip, heatmap, matrix, live-code cell, quiz) rather than hand-built one-offs like Ciechanowski's essays (https://ciechanow.ski/).
Evidence caveats: most interview-format data comes from secondary blogs and aggregators; several price and star figures are secondhand; re-verify before quoting publicly.
